source.label: CA Official Voter Information Guide, Nov 3 2026 (Secretary of State)

1.title: Authorizes Bonds for Housing Affordability Programs
1.title_official: AUTHORIZES BONDS FOR HOUSING AFFORDABILITY PROGRAMS
1.placed_by: Put on the Ballot by the Legislature
1.summary: Authorizes $11.25 billion in state general obligation bonds for housing affordability programs, including multifamily rental housing, mortgages for veterans, supportive housing, preservation of existing affordable housing, and downpayment assistance.
1.fiscal: Increased state cost of $500 million to $600 million annually for about 25 years to repay the housing bond.
1.supporters: US Vets; CA Federation of Teachers; Self-Help for the Elderly; Habitat for Humanity CA; CA Alliance of Child & Family Services
1.yes_means: The state could borrow $11.25 billion to support veterans and affordable housing.
1.no_means: The state could not borrow $11.25 billion to support veterans and affordable housing.
1.argument_pro: Prop. 1 builds affordable homes for veterans, seniors, people with disabilities, low- and middle-income working families, vulnerable Californians and essential workers—teachers, firefighters and nurses. Expands homeownership opportunities, fast-tracks affordable shovel-ready homes, helps those one crisis away from homelessness. Requires strict fiscal accountability and public oversight with no new taxes.
1.argument_con: NO ARGUMENT AGAINST PROPOSITION 1 WAS SUBMITTED.

2.title: Increases State’s Rainy Day Fund
2.placed_by: Put on the Ballot by the Legislature
2.summary: Increases California's Rainy Day Fund, approved by voters in 2014, to provide funding for education, health care, public safety, and other essential services during economic downturns.
2.fiscal: State budget reserves would be higher.
2.supporters: CA Professional Firefighters; LA Chamber of Commerce; Gavin Newsom; Xavier Becerra; Assemblymember Jesse Gabriel
2.yes_means: Rules for building state budget reserves and paying down extra state debts would change. As a result, state budget reserves would be higher. The state also would be required to make extra debt payments for longer.
2.no_means: Rules for building state budget reserves and paying down extra state debts would not change.
2.argument_pro: Vote yes on Proposition 2 to protect schools, healthcare, and public safety funding. Proposition 2 doubles the state's Rainy Day Fund, stops politicians from overspending when there is a budget surplus, and ensures education funding continues during economic downturns. It has bipartisan support from firefighters, hospitals, health clinics, and educators.
2.argument_con: Proposition 2 guarantees more spending, not savings, creating a loophole that makes taxpayer rebates less likely by excluding reserve deposits from California's constitutional spending limit. It provides no new funding for education, healthcare, or public safety. Vote No to protect taxpayer rebates and constitutional limits.

3.title: Provides Permanent Funding for Schools and Health Care by Extending Existing Tax on High Incomes
3.title_official: PROVIDES PERMANENT FUNDING FOR SCHOOLS AND HEALTH CARE BY EXTENDING EXISTING TAX ON HIGH INCOMES
3.placed_by: Put on the Ballot by Petition Signatures
3.summary: Makes permanent existing voter-approved tax rates for individuals earning over $371,000 (adjusted annually for inflation). Allocates tax revenues to public education.
3.fiscal: Maintains $5 billion to $15 billion of annual state income tax revenue by making a temporary tax increase on high-income earners permanent instead of letting it expire in 2031.
3.supporters: California Teachers Association; CA School Nurses Organization; California State PTA; Planned Parenthood Affiliates of CA
3.opponents: California Taxpayers Association; Family Business Association of California; California Hispanic Chambers of Commerce
3.yes_means: An income tax increase on high-income earners in place since 2012 would become permanent instead of expiring in 2031.
3.no_means: An income tax increase on high-income earners in place since 2012 would expire in 2031.
3.argument_pro: PROPOSITION 3 PROTECTS OUR SCHOOLS AND HEALTHCARE WITHOUT RAISING YOUR TAXES. Prop. 3 prevents a massive tax cut for millionaires and billionaires by maintaining the current tax rates the wealthiest 2% have paid for 15 years and requires strict accountability and audits to ensure school funding gets to classrooms. Vote YES.
3.argument_con: Californians already pay the nation’s highest income, sales, and gas taxes—and have the highest cost of living. Prop. 3 makes temporary income taxes permanent while Sacramento wastes billions on failed programs instead of voters’ priorities. Don’t reward failure. Fix spending first before making taxes permanent. No on Prop. 3.

4.title: Repeals Prohibition Against Public Funding of Election Campaigns
4.title_official: REPEALS PROHIBITION AGAINST PUBLIC FUNDING OF ELECTION CAMPAIGNS
4.placed_by: Put on the Ballot by the Legislature
4.summary: Repeals prohibition on state and local governments offering public funding of candidate election campaigns. Public funding programs may not use funds earmarked for education, transportation, or public safety.
4.fiscal: Ongoing costs to the state of a few hundred thousand dollars each year for the Fair Political Practices Commission to answer questions from state and local governments about public campaign finance programs.
4.supporters: League of Women Voters of CA; California Nurses Association; Mental Health Advocacy; Social Security Works; Consumer Watchdog
4.opponents: California Taxpayers Assn; Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Assn; Family Business Assn of California; United Latinos Action
4.yes_means: State and local governments could create public campaign financing programs for public office candidates, subject to limits on which public funds could be used, how the public funds could be used, and who could receive them.
4.no_means: State and most local governments would remain unable to create public campaign finance programs for public office candidates.
4.argument_pro: YES ON 4. California is the ONLY state that bans public funding of campaigns— communities in all other 49 states have this right. Special interests want to keep the ban to protect their power. Prop. 4 removes it. Strict taxpayer safeguards. Vote YES: Elections should be won, not bought.
4.argument_con: Prop. 4 allows politicians to use YOUR taxpayer money to fund their negative campaigns. Prop. 4 has NO LIMIT on the number of candidates who can get taxpayer money and NO LIMIT on how much taxpayer money they can get. Worse yet, Prop. 4 allows SPECIAL INTEREST MONEY IN POLITICS. NO ON PROP. 4.

5.title: Changes Recall Election Process for Statewide Officers
5.title_official: CHANGES RECALL ELECTION PROCESS FOR STATEWIDE OFFICERS
5.placed_by: Put on the Ballot by the Legislature
5.summary: Under current law, voters elect replacement candidates at the same time as the recall election. This measure instead fills recall vacancies by subsequent special election or appointment.
5.fiscal: Net fiscal effect unknown. In the event of a recall, savings or costs of millions of dollars to administer the election depending on the office recalled.
5.yes_means: Recall elections would no longer include a question about who should fill the vacancy. Instead, vacancies typically would be filled through special elections or appointments, depending on the office and timing.
5.no_means: Voters would continue to be asked who should fill the vacancy as part of recall elections.
5.argument_pro: Proposition 5 restores the recall to its original purpose: removing corrupt officials. It closes the loophole that allows replacements to win with a small fraction of the vote, reducing the politics and costs of future recalls. Endorsed by League of Women Voters of California and California Common Cause. Vote YES
5.argument_con: Proposition 5 degrades California’s century-old recall process by limiting voters’ right to select a replacement for recalled officials. Instead, when statewide elected officials are recalled, other politicians would choose a replacement. For lower offices, another costly, taxpayer-funded election would come months later, leaving the office vacant and the people unrepresented.

37.title: Creates Loan Program for Middle-income Buyers of Qualified New Homes
37.title_official: CREATES LOAN PROGRAM FOR MIDDLE-INCOME BUYERS OF QUALIFIED NEW HOMES
37.placed_by: Put on the Ballot by Petition Signatures
37.summary: Authorizes $25 billion in bonds to offer eligible buyers fixed-rate mortgages for up to 17% of purchase price of a newly constructed home priced below about $1.5 million. Borrowers must be California residents, occupy the home, meet income limits, and pay at least 3% down. Bonds repaid by mortgage payments, not State.
37.fiscal: No direct state or local costs.
37.supporters: United Nurses Associations of California; California Conference of Carpenters; California State Treasurer Fiona Ma
37.yes_means: The state would create a new homebuying assistance program. The state could sell up to $25 billion in revenue bonds to fund the program. Bonds would be paid back by homeowners’ payments on their home loans.
37.no_means: The state would not be required to create a new homebuying assistance program.
37.argument_pro: Zero Taxpayer Cost—No Taxpayer Risk. Prop. 37 makes buying a home more affordable, keeping homeownership attainable for hardworking and middle-class Californians, with low-interest mortgages funded by private bond investors, NOT TAXPAYERS. Must be CA resident to qualify, meet income requirements, occupy home, make monthly payments, repay loan. Strict accountability/audits.
37.argument_con: NO ARGUMENT AGAINST PROPOSITION 37 WAS SUBMITTED.

38.title: Authorizes Bonds for Immunology Medical Research
38.title_official: AUTHORIZES BONDS FOR IMMUNOLOGY MEDICAL RESEARCH
38.placed_by: Put on the Ballot by Petition Signatures
38.summary: Authorizes $8.4 billion in general obligation bonds for immunology and immunotherapy research, half to a single University of California-affiliated nonprofit medical research institute, half to research grants.
38.fiscal: Increased state cost of $500 million to $600 million annually for about 20 years to repay the research bond, with some or all of the cost offset if the funded research generates revenue.
38.supporters: Michael J. Fox Foundation; Alzheimer’s Los Angeles; Kidney Cancer Assoc; American Nurses Assoc\CA
38.yes_means: The state could borrow $8.4 billion to support medical research in immunology and immunotherapy conducted by California research institutes and universities.
38.no_means: The state could not borrow $8.4 billion to support medical research in immunology and immunotherapy conducted by California research institutes and universities.
38.argument_pro: YES on 38 supports life-saving immunology research to cure and prevent diseases like cancer, heart disease, Alzheimer’s. Strong accountability including independent audits. Mandates 20% Rx discount. Designed to ensure no cost to taxpayers. YES on 38 could save your life and someone you love. Alzheimer’s Association, The Michael J. Fox Foundation for Parkinson’s Research urge YES on 38! www.YESon38.com
38.argument_con: California should continue supporting biomedical research, but Proposition 38 is the wrong approach. It would commit taxpayers to decades of new bond debt while limiting California’s flexibility to address changing health priorities. Research funding should be guided through the normal budget process—not by ballot initiatives.

39.title: Prohibits Citizens from Voting unless They Present Government-issued Identification
39.title_official: PROHIBITS CITIZENS FROM VOTING UNLESS THEY PRESENT GOVERNMENT-ISSUED IDENTIFICATION
39.placed_by: Put on the Ballot by Petition Signatures
39.summary: Invalidates mail ballots that do not have last four digits of designated government-issued identification number written on envelope. Prohibits in-person voting without presenting government-issued identification.
39.fiscal: Costs of between tens of millions of dollars and low hundreds of millions of dollars each year to implement new voting requirements.
39.supporters: The Transparency Foundation; Latino American Political Assn; Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Assn; CA Women’s Leadership Assn
39.opponents: ACLU California Action; Common Cause; League of Women Voters of California
39.yes_means: Voters would be required to present additional identifying information to elections officials each time they vote.
39.no_means: A voter’s identity would continue to be established with the voter’s signature.
39.argument_pro: Yes on Prop. 39 gives California a BIPARTISAN solution for VOTER ID. Supported by a solid majority of Democratic, Independent and Republican voters. Increases trust and confidence in our elections.
39.argument_con: No on Prop. 39. This would advance Trump’s voter suppression agenda by adding costly, unnecessary barriers that could block eligible California voters, expose personal information to identity theft, and waste hundreds of millions in taxpayer dollars. Don’t let MAGA billionaires decide which voters count. Vote No.

40.title: Imposes One-time Tax on Certain Taxpayers
40.title_official: IMPOSES ONE-TIME TAX ON CERTAIN TAXPAYERS
40.placed_by: Put on the Ballot by Petition Signatures
40.summary: Imposes 5% tax on certain taxpayers with assets over $1 billion; revenue primarily for health care. Exempts revenues from constitutional requirements for school funding and spending limit.
40.fiscal: Temporary revenue increase of tens of billions of dollars spread over several years from wealth tax on billionaires. Possible ongoing decrease of less than $1 billion per year in income tax revenue from billionaires.
40.supporters: US Senator Bernie Sanders; SEIU United Healthcare Workers West
40.opponents: California Primary Care Association; California School Boards Association; California Taxpayers Association
40.yes_means: The state would collect a one-time tax from billionaires equal to 5 percent of their wealth.
40.no_means: The state would not collect a one-time tax from billionaires equal to 5 percent of their wealth.
40.argument_pro: Vote YES on 40 to tax billionaires. Trump slashed healthcare funding to pay for billionaire tax breaks, eliminating coverage for over a million Californians and doubling health insurance premiums for millions more. It’s time to make billionaires pay their fair share and stop sticking the middle class with the bill.
40.argument_con: Prop. 40 is a flawed, one-time tax scheme that hurts our economy, damages our state budget, and contains a loophole exposing all Californians to taxes we can’t afford—but does nothing to lower healthcare costs. No safeguards, no accountability. Join California Teachers Association, California Medical Association, California Children’s Hospital Association, California Professional Firefighters, State Building and Construction Trades Council of California, Democrats and Republicans: NO on 40.

41.title: Prohibits New State Taxes that Exclude Revenues from State Spending Limit. Requires Audits for New State Special Taxes
41.title_official: PROHIBITS NEW STATE TAXES THAT EXCLUDE REVENUES FROM STATE SPENDING LIMIT. REQUIRES AUDITS FOR NEW STATE SPECIAL TAXES
41.placed_by: Put on the Ballot by Petition Signatures
41.summary: Nullifies state taxes enacted after January 1, 2026 that exempt their revenues from voter-approved state spending limit. Requires pre-election and recurring audits of programs funded by new special taxes.
41.fiscal: The net fiscal effect is unknown as it depends on future decisions by voters, the Legislature, and other policymakers.
41.supporters: CA Society of Certified Public Accountants (CalCPAs); CalAsian Chamber of Commerce; California Taxpayers Association (CalTax)
41.opponents: US Senator Bernie Sanders; SEIU United Healthcare Workers West
41.yes_means: When special taxes are proposed by voter initiatives, the California State Auditor would review programs funded by the tax before the initiative appears on the ballot. The California State Auditor also would regularly review programs funded by special taxes approved by voters or the Legislature. In addition, the state might not be able to exclude any new special tax spending from its spending limit.
41.no_means: The California State Auditor’s responsibility to review government programs would not change. The state spending limit requirements would not change.
41.argument_pro: Californians deserve better results for our taxes. Billions have flowed into programs like homelessness, with too little to show for it. Prop. 41 requires the independent State Auditor to conduct PUBLIC AUDITS of programs funded by new taxes—so we get more transparency, more accountability and better outcomes for taxpayers.
41.argument_con: Prop. 41 isn’t really about audits—it’s a billionaire-funded trick designed to undo the California Billionaire Tax. Billionaires would rather millions of Californians lose healthcare than pay a modest tax on their extreme wealth. Don’t fall for the billionaires’ lies. Vote NO on 41.

42.title: Prohibits New State Personal Property Taxes and Certain Retroactive State Taxes
42.title_official: PROHIBITS NEW STATE PERSONAL PROPERTY TAXES AND CERTAIN RETROACTIVE STATE TAXES
42.placed_by: Put on the Ballot by Petition Signatures
42.summary: Prohibits any new state tax (1) imposed on the ownership of personal property (all things people own other than real estate), or (2) that applies retroactively based on taxpayer’s past activities. Nullifies taxes enacted after January 1, 2026 that conflict with this measure.
42.fiscal: Possibility that tax revenues will not go up as much in the future.
42.supporters: CA Professional Firefighters; State Building & Construction Trades Council of CA; AMVETS Department of CA
42.opponents: US Senator Bernie Sanders; SEIU United Healthcare Workers West
42.yes_means: The state could not establish new taxes on the ownership of financial assets or other personal property.
42.no_means: The state would continue to have the option to establish new taxes on the ownership of financial assets or other personal property.
42.argument_pro: California’s Constitution currently allows the Legislature to tax retirement and savings—even though you already paid taxes on that money when you earned it! Prop. 42 protects Californians from this double taxation, by prohibiting new and retroactive taxes on personal property, including retirement and savings. You earned it. Prop. 42 protects it.
42.argument_con: This is just another billionaire-funded trick. Prop. 42 isn’t really about protecting your retirement savings—its only real purpose is to undo the California Billionaire Tax. Billionaires would rather millions of Californians lose healthcare than pay a modest tax on their extreme wealth. Vote NO on 42.

43.title: Limits Voters’ Ability to Raise Revenues for Local Government Services
43.title_official: LIMITS VOTERS’ ABILITY TO RAISE REVENUES FOR LOCAL GOVERNMENT SERVICES
43.placed_by: Put on the Ballot by the Legislature
43.summary: Limits voters’ ability to pass voter-proposed local special taxes by increasing percentage of votes needed to approve such ballot measures from a majority (over 50%) to two-thirds, beginning January 1, 2027.
43.fiscal: Possibility that local government tax revenues will not go up as much in the future due to a higher vote threshold for certain taxes.
43.supporters: California Taxpayers Association; Family Business Association of California; California Hispanic Chambers of Commerce
43.opponents: California Professional Firefighters; California Federation of Teachers; Nurse Alliance of SEIU CA.
43.yes_means: Certain local government taxes would require two-thirds approval by voters.
43.no_means: Certain local government taxes could continue to be approved by voters with a majority vote.
43.argument_pro: Prop. 43 protects taxpayers by restoring Proposition 13’s two-thirds vote requirement to pass local special taxes, including sales taxes, real estate taxes and utility taxes. Courts have allowed special interests to pass earmarked tax increases with fewer votes. Prop. 43 closes this loophole, protecting taxpayers, homeowners and renters. Vote yes.
43.argument_con: PROPOSITION 43 LIMITS VOTERS’ ABILITY TO FUND ESSENTIAL LOCAL SERVICES including fire protection, 911 response, schools, roads, hospitals and affordable housing. It doesn’t cut your taxes and lets just 33.4% of voters veto what nearly 67% want. Protect your vote and majority rule. Vote NO on Proposition 43.

44.title: Requires Community Health Clinics Spend 90% of Revenue on Program Services
44.title_official: REQUIRES COMMUNITY HEALTH CLINICS SPEND 90% OF REVENUE ON PROGRAM SERVICES
44.placed_by: Put on the Ballot by Petition Signatures
44.summary: Imposes penalties on nonprofit Federally Qualified Health Centers (community clinics providing primary care to medically underserved areas and populations) that spend less than 90% of revenue on “program services” advancing their charitable purpose, including but not limited to patient services.
44.fiscal: Increased state costs in the low tens of millions of dollars per year, covered by fees.
44.opponents: American Academy of Pediatrics CA; CA School Nurses Org; CA Academy of Family Physicians; CA Medical Assoc.
44.yes_means: Certain private nonprofit health care clinics would have to spend at least 90 percent of their revenue each year on providing health care services.
44.no_means: The new requirement on health care clinic spending would not go into effect.
44.argument_pro: Prop. 44 holds community clinics and their executives accountable by requiring that 90% of clinic revenue be spent on clinics’ charitable mission: patient care and services that make care possible. It increases transparency, reduces wasteful executive spending, and ensures healthcare dollars go where they belong: caring for Californians in need.
44.argument_con: Prop. 44 is a dangerous measure that will shut down hundreds of community health clinics and eliminate vital patient services for millions of Californians. American Academy of Pediatrics CA, California Medical Association, California Academy of Family Physicians, California School Nurses Organization, doctors, nurses and patients urge NO on 44! www.NOProp44.com

45.title: Modifies Environmental Review for Certain Projects
45.title_official: MODIFIES ENVIRONMENTAL REVIEW FOR CERTAIN PROJECTS
45.placed_by: Put on the Ballot by Petition Signatures
45.summary: Amends California Environmental Quality Act (CEQA) to expedite environmental review for certain projects (including most housing, transportation, water, and health projects) by setting deadlines to complete environmental review and resolve lawsuits challenging project approvals.
45.fiscal: Initial costs for state and local governments, likely in the high tens of millions of dollars—potentially exceeding $100 million—annually, partly covered by fees. Uncertain, potentially more significant positive or negative longer-term fiscal effects.
45.supporters: California Children’s Hospital Association; California Water Association; California Council for Affordable Housing
45.opponents: Coalition for Clean Air; CA Environmental Voters; Physicians for Social Responsibility, LA; National Wildlife Federation
45.yes_means: Certain public and private projects would be eligible for new project review and court challenge procedures. For example, new procedures would tighten time limits for environmental review and reduce the scope of what courts can consider when reviewing legal challenges.
45.no_means: Public and private projects would continue to use existing project review and court challenge procedures.
45.argument_pro: The failing status quo is making California unaffordable. Prop. 45 fixes our broken system and lowers our high cost of living by cutting red tape to build housing, water, schools, hospitals, clean energy, and wildfire prevention faster—while maintaining California’s strong environmental protections. Vote YES for a more affordable California. YESonProp45.com
45.argument_con: PROPOSITION 45 LIMITS ENVIRONMENTAL AND PUBLIC REVIEW OF PROJECTS BUILT IN YOUR COMMUNITY. It guts The California Environmental Quality Act—flipping California law to protect corporate profits over public health and our air and water. Prop. 45 won’t lower your costs: its utility and corporate funders profit while taxpayers pay more. VOTE NO.
